wins.biggestWin: Make the desk a real two-column plane in every state, not only in seam and pressure, and give the index plane a ground of its own. Today the resting frame — the one a venue owner sees for 95% of her session — is a 1000px white rectangle holding 527px of writing, with the privacy line marooned 240px out to the right, sitting on a white sheet above a list on the same white, separated by one 9%-ink hairline and 19px of ghost paper. That is a compose box over a grouped list: it is the shape of Bear, Apple Notes and Craft, and it is where the "extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words" risk is still live. It is not live in the seam, where the note holds the left column and everything true about it holds a ruled margin — that frame is the only one that could not belong to another product. Promote that composition to the default (margin column carrying the filing chip, the privacy line and the two capture verbs; foot shrinks to the writing column), and lay the lower plane on its own ground (ink at 0.02 from the index head to the foot of the sheet, edge to edge inside the sheet, with the desk's --paper shadow falling onto it). Two changes, both inside the palette and the locked architecture, and the resting frame stops being a box on a list and starts being a desk above an index — which is what the founder locked and what the CSS comments already claim.

Rebuild the index row as a phone object rather than the desktop row squeezed into 308px. One element, three of the five defects above: the clamp that slices a glyph and orphans its ellipsis, the day heading that becomes indistinguishable from the row lede, and the semibold that is spent on every line. Word-safe the trim inline with the sentence, move the day heading into the uppercase micro-label register, and drop the lede to one weight — after that the phone index reads like Things' list instead of a desktop table that has been narrowed. Beyond the defects, the thing this product should have and does not is a date register. "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" is the single fact a venue operator and a couple orient by, and it appears three times on one screen in three settings — 13/400/-0.012em in the head, 13/600/-0.006em in the day heading, and 12/400 tabular as "35 minutes ago" in the row — with no two agreeing on weight or tracking. A wedding product whose whole world is one date should own a date the way Things owns one: a single declared setting, recognisable anywhere in the product, so that the date is a thing the reader knows on sight rather than a string the layout happens to be carrying. The remaining distance to 9.5 is craft debt, not a limit of this direction; the desktop resting, reading, seam and voice states are already at 8.8, and the phone is a round behind them.

Let a note be written on a second visit. Everything here is built for the first three seconds and nothing for minute four: the desk's read body is a P, not a field, so a venue owner whose note reads "Ask the venue whether the ballroom can be accessed from 8am" and who gets the answer on Tuesday has nowhere to put it — her only move is a new note, and the index gains a second row that looks exactly like the first. Making the desk's read body the same field the top sheet already is (same measure, same 17px, same Ctrl+Enter, same undo, "edited" already exists in the desk facts) costs nothing architecturally — the desk is defined as where you write — and it pays three times: it closes the missing moment, it retires the false "still yours to edit" on the crossing receipt, and it gives the index a reason to exist beyond an archive. To be explicit about the rest of the distance: the five defects above are craft debt and a day closes all of them. This is not. It is a scope call this direction has quietly made, and no further polish round will reach it. And to answer the failure mode directly — this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The head leads with the house's next Saturday, the grouping is by event rather than folder, the honesty states are written for someone standing in a marquee with no signal, and the seam exists because a venue owner's note has a job inside it. The wedding is in the bones. The limit is that a capture instrument this good stops at capture.

Make the head's subject live and let it scope the whole notebook, then scope the hand to it. What is left between this build and 9.5 is not mostly defects; it is the absence of one moment. The product knows the house is facing Mara & Finn on Saturday, prints it in its biggest type, and then does nothing with it: the pile is still the whole notebook, the hand still deals the whole notebook, and the same string is repeated inertly as a group heading below. Give that line a press, scope both planes and the review queue to it, and the review room stops being a generic inbox of eight and becomes \"three things left before Saturday\" — which is the difference between a very well made notes app that contains wedding words and a venue's notebook. The direction can do this; it needs no new colour, weight or plane. Fix defer-lowers-the-count regardless, because that one is a straight contradiction between what the screen says and what the product says out loud, and it is reachable in two clicks.

Put every visible string through the same gate the pixels have already been through seven times. The craft on this build is real — the resting frame reads like Bear, the dictation floor is better than anything Things or iA ships, and the subject axis (Mara & Finn, The house, The course) is genuinely venue-shaped rather than a notes app wearing wedding words. The distance to 9.5 is not the architecture and it is not the pixels; it is that the language never got a round of its own. Four product-owned strings were silently rewritten at render time and the one that mattered most was rewritten upward into a promise the product cannot keep; one word (\"kept\") means two different things at the same instant; one state has three names; the search sentence is ungrammatical at n=1. Concretely: make notes-copy.ts the only source of visible text (push the lab's three good rewrites back into the module as keys), fix the register — one verb per act, one noun per state, one name for where a thought belongs, used identically in the badge, the button, the strip and the announcement — and add copy assertions to the behaviour gate: no rendered string absent from the module, plural agreement checked at 0/1/2, and no two strings naming the same state. That single pass closes findings 1, 2 and 5, removes the contradiction between what is drawn and what is spoken, and takes the seam's vocabulary problem from a symptom to a decision. This is craft debt, not a limit of the direction — one more round closes it.

Restore the peel as a real second piece of paper on the desk. Delete the `.top[data-two] .deskAside .peel` override at master.css:887–888, give it back its shadow, its padding, its own smaller edge and a notch pointing at the note it came from, and add a 260ms peel-in keyframe alongside `arrive`. Right now the product's signature promise — the note never leaves, only the words you pick cross — is drawn properly exactly once, in the review hand, and flattened into a share sidebar in the room where most people will meet it, for the stated reason that it left the sheet's lower third empty. That is a taste trade made in the wrong direction. To answer the panel's standing question plainly: this is not an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words — the seam, the still-to-decide spine and the honesty line are genuinely operator-shaped, and the copy is the best-judged thing in the build. But it is close to becoming one, because the two moments that carry the emotional weight are the two that are least finished: the peel is a sidebar and the dictation floor is a still photograph with a hard-coded 0:07 on it. Neither of those is craft debt another round will grind away; both are decisions, and both are reversible in a day. Fix them and this reaches 9.2 or better. Leave them and no amount of further gate-passing moves it, because what is missing is not a defect — it is the moment where a person watches their own sentence become a task and believes the rest of the page stayed hers.

Make the hand deal by the day the house is facing. Everything else on my list returns the build to a standard it already sets for itself; this one adds something it does not have. The index already sorts by stake then days (notebook.js:1225-1232) and the head already prints \"in 2 days\", but queue() (notebook.js:382) hands the operator her decisions in the order the notes happened to arrive — the Saturday ballroom question, then a studio newsletter idea with no date, while two more Saturday decisions wait behind it. Give queue() that same comparator and print the subject and its distance on the card, and the deciding surface stops being a generic review queue and starts being a venue's Friday. That is the difference between an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it and one whose behaviour is shaped by the wedding. On the rest: the distance to 9.5 is craft debt, not a limit of this direction. The 1440 rooms are close to 9 already — the desk/index composition, the seam, the honesty room and the copy are all at the level named. What holds it at 8.4 is a phone that is a full grade below the other three viewports (a two-line black \"8 still to decide\" pill dominating the head, the house name dropped from it entirely, the last row permanently under the dock), one timer-driven repaint that drops keyboard focus to <body>, one selection state that is invisible in the room that most needs it, and smaller residue I could not fit in five: the capture announces \"Kept.\" while the strip beside it says \"Saved.\" and \"Kept\" already names a different decision in the index and the hand; the desk margin counts a person's words twice on one card (\"14 words picked\" as prose, \"LENGTH / 30 words\" as a spec row) after the read-back was fixed for exactly that; every note whose text ends in a full stop gets a double period in its accessible name (notebook.js:1183, and again in the pick announcement); and the pressure room's 36 notes are 14 notes repeated modulo (data.js:280), so three consecutive rows carry identical text and the room built to prove density instead reads as a duplication bug. Another round closes all of it.

confirmed.element: .handBody inside .handTop, ?state=review, card 2 of 8 (press K then T)
confirmed.problem: The hand card is a fixed 272px frame and .handBody is its only flexible child with overflow:auto and no min-height. When the nudge line is added on a refused T, the body is squeezed to exactly 0px high (measured: rect 181->181, text still in the DOM and still in the accessible name). The card then reads: title, "Written · 5 hours ago", a boxed instruction saying "Pick the words in the note that should become the task", and 190px of empty white where the note used to be. The product is asking a venue owner to pick words in a note it has just erased from the screen, and the one card in the hand that is meant to be the note itself becomes a card about nothing. Card 1 does not do this, so the failure is silent and intermittent.
confirmed.fix: Give .handBody a min-height of 3 lines (calc(var(--lh-read) * 3em)) and let the card grow instead of the body shrinking: change .handTop from a fixed height to min-height with the same value, and cap the body at max-height: 46vh with its existing overflow:auto so a long note scrolls rather than the card growing without limit. Verify by asserting in notes-interaction-check that .handBody.getBoundingClientRect().height >= 40 on every card in the hand, before and after T and K.
confirmed.verdict: Reproduced live in Chromium at 1440x960. ?state=review, press K then T (card 2 of 8, no standing pick): .handBody goes from rect {top 181, h 84} at rest to {top 181, bottom 181, h 0} after the refusal, while .handTop stays locked at 272px. Child geometry after T: handQ 25.6, readSrc 17.4, handBody 0, nudge 59.7, handFoot 53. .handTop is height:272px with .handBody the only flex:1 child (master.css:756-762) and no min-height, so the nudge is paid for entirely out of the note. Screenshot confirms: the card shows the title, "Written . 5 hours ago", the boxed "Pick the words in the note that should become the task. Only those cross." and no note at all. The product asks a venue owner to pick words in a note it erased in the same repaint. Card 1 has a standing pick so T peels instead, which is why the failure is silent and why six rounds missed it. Not already handled: no min-height on .handBody anywhere; the same guard already exists on .topField (master.css:392), so the fix is the file's own idiom. Not covered by the gate: notes-interaction-check.mjs:1362/1370/1393 assert the pick is drawn, absent, and walkable, and the refusal is gated for copy, glyph and focus return, but nothing asserts the body has non-zero height and no assertion runs after the refusal. No constraint breach: no hue, no weight, no architecture change. Two corrections that do not soften it: (1) there is not "190px of empty white" - the nudge and its margins reclaim most of the interior, the real dead band is ~35px plus the unused right half of the measure; (2) the proposed swap of .handTop from height to min-height would reintroduce the queue bob the fixed height was introduced to kill, per the source comment at master.css:754.
confirmed.sharpenedFix: Keep .handTop at height: 272px so the resting queue never bobs (the reason the fixed height exists, per the comment at master.css:754), and let the card grow only in the refusal state. Add: .handBody { min-height: calc(var(--lh-read) * 3em); max-height: 46vh; } - 3 lines is exactly the 84px the body already occupies at rest, so nothing moves until a nudge appears - and .handTop:has(.nudge) { height: auto; min-height: 272px; } so only the refused card grows, by the nudge's ~60px, and a long note scrolls inside the body rather than growing the card. This mirrors the guard already shipped on .topField (master.css:392). Gate it in notes-interaction-check.mjs: walk all 8 cards in the hand and assert .handBody.getBoundingClientRect().height >= 40 at rest AND after T on every one, including the pickless cards where T refuses.

confirmed.element: .undo (position:absolute; bottom:78px) over .index at any scroll offset other than the end

At scrollTop 0 with the strip live, the ink pill sits directly on top of two rows: measured, .undo occupies 818->864 and intersects "Quote from today that I want to keep…" and "Follow up with the motion designer about the venue film", cutting the second sentence into three visible pieces (words, black pill, "…hoice before she can lock…") with the status pill and timestamp still showing to its right. An opaque control painting over a person's own writing is the checklist defect, and it happens on the single most common path in the product: capture, then look at the pile.
confirmed.fix: Stop padding the scroller and start shortening it. While .sheet[data-undo] is set, subtract the strip's band from the index's height rather than adding it to its padding: .sheet[data-undo] .indexWrap { padding-bottom: 58px } with .index keeping its existing 132px foot padding, so the strip lives in reserved layout space below the scroll box and no row can ever pass under it. Assert in notes-interaction-check that no .idxRow rect intersects the .undo rect at scrollTop 0, mid-scroll and at the end.
confirmed.verdict: Verified live in Playwright at 1440x960. After Ctrl+Enter the .undo strip measures 818->864 while the .index scroll box runs to 942, so the strip's entire band lies inside the scroller's viewport. The pile's natural resting position after a keep is scrollTop 0 (the new row lands at the top), so with no user action at all the ink pill paints across "Follow up with the motion designer about the venue film…", cutting it into three visible pieces with its status pill and timestamp still showing to the right; one row is still covered at mid-scroll. master.css:482 reserves the band as trailing padding inside the scroller, which only clears the LAST row at the END, exactly as the finding says — while the comment at master.css:624-629 claims the pile is "shorter by exactly its height… at every scroll position", which the code does not do. The behaviour gate does not cover it: notes-interaction-check.mjs:1633-1648 sets idx.scrollTop = idx.scrollHeight before asserting non-intersection, so it tests only the end. This is the checklist's "controls painting over content", on the most common path in the product, and no non-negotiable constraint is involved.
confirmed.sharpenedFix: Correct the arithmetic before implementing: the strip sits at bottom:78px and is 46px tall, so the reserved band is 124px, not 58px. Shortening the scroller by 58px leaves its bottom at 884, still below the strip's top at 818, and rows keep passing under it. Move the reservation out of the scroller without changing the total: .sheet[data-undo] .indexWrap { padding-bottom: 124px } and .sheet[data-undo] .index { padding-bottom: 8px }, dropping --undo-pad from the .index padding entirely. Total reserved foot stays 132px whether the strip is live or not, so the pile does not jump when the strip appears or expires, the dock no longer overlaps the shortened scroll box (which is what the 132px was for), and the strip lives in layout space no row can enter. Mirror the same two numbers in the three width blocks (master.css:1113-1119 and 1215-1216, where the strip moves to bottom:88px, giving a 134px band). Then widen the round-6 assertion: run the no-intersection check at scrollTop 0, at mid-scroll and at the end, at 390, 768 and 1440, and assert on rows that are actually inside the scroller's viewport rect.

confirmed.element: .handTop in ?state=review, across cards and across T
confirmed.problem: The hand's card is content-sized and centred, so its width is set by whichever row of controls is longest. Measured at 1440: card 1 is 767.3px (377.3->1144.7), card 2 is 838.5px (341.8->1180.3), and pressing T on card 1 shrinks it to 617px (452.5->1069.5). Deciding a card therefore slides the frame 35px sideways, and refusing one slides the note's own words 75px to the right while they are being read. A hand of cards has to be one stable frame that the cards pass through; this one breathes on every keystroke. It also shares no edge with the index below it (card left 377 vs row text 294), so the review room has three left axes stacked in one view.
confirmed.fix: Fix the frame instead of the content: .handTop { width: min(100%, calc(var(--measure) + 276px + 34px + 48px)) } — the same writing column plus margin the desk already resolves to — and let .handFoot wrap inside it. The card then sits on the desk's own column, its left edge lands on 261 like the paper, and the pips, body and actions stop moving between cards.
confirmed.verdict:
CONFIRMED — I tried to kill this and could not. Every measurement reproduces exactly.

SOURCE. `master.css:282` — `.desk { display: flex; justify-content: center; }`. In review, `.desk`'s only child is `.hand`, a flex item with default `flex: 0 1 auto`, so its width is max-content. `.handStack` and `.handTop` inherit that. The card's frame is therefore set by whichever row of controls happens to be longest.

MEASURED at 1440 (Playwright, live file, ?state=review):
- card 1: `.handTop` 377.3 → 1144.7, w 767.3
- press K, card 2: 341.8 → 1180.3, w 838.5 (frame slides 35.5px left)
- press T on card 1: 452.5 → 1069.5, w 617.0 (frame slides 75.2px right)
- `.handBody` left goes 403.3 → 478.5 on that T press. The note's own words move 75px sideways at the exact moment the peel opens — in the one room whose architectural promise is that the note is never covered. It is not covered; it is moved out from under the reader.
- Identical widths at 1280 and 1920 (767.3 → 838.5 after K at both), confirming pure max-content sizing with no viewport relationship at all.

NOT ALREADY HANDLED, AND THE BUILD'S OWN LOGIC INDICTS IT. `master.css:753-757` carries the comment "A fixed height, because the card is a card in a hand: working the queue made the second plane bob by 34px on every keystroke as each note's length changed the card under it" — they diagnosed exactly this failure on the vertical axis, fixed it with `height: 272px`, and left the horizontal axis running free at 71px and 150px, four times the bob they judged unacceptable.

NOT A RESTATEMENT OF THE GATE. `scripts/design/notes-interaction-check.mjs:1013-1029` asserts "the desk and the index share a column" at 1280/1440/1920 — but it opens `""`, the notebook state, and queries `.pile`. The review room has no `.pile`. The gate enforces the exact principle this finding names and never visits the room that breaks it.

THE OUTLIER IS REAL, NOT TASTE. I measured `.desk > *` across every other state: notebook, capture, readback, seam, pressure, nothing, not-yet all sit at left 261, width 1000, dead stable, against `.idxRow` at 251/1020 and the head word at 261. Review is the only room in the product where the desk plane does not land on 261, and the only one where it moves at all. Three left axes in one view (261 head/index, 294 row text, 377→452 card) is not a stylistic preference next to eight states that agree.

IN SCOPE. No colour, no weight, no architectural change — a hand of cards stays a hand of cards; it just stops breathing.
confirmed.sharpenedFix:
Put the width on `.hand`, not `.handTop` — `.handTop`'s `min(100%, …)` resolves its percentage against an indefinite-width flex ancestor and will not reliably constrain `.hand` itself. Set `.hand { width: min(100%, 1000px); }` expressed in the desk's own terms — the same `var(--measure) + 34px column-gap + 276px margin` plus the paper's padding that `.top[data-two]` (master.css:319-325) already resolves to — so the card lands on 261 like every other plane and `.deckNote` and the absolutely-positioned `.handCard` stack follow it for free.

Two things to check when landing it, both consequences of the frame no longer flexing to the content:
1. `.handFoot` already has `flex-wrap: wrap`, but `.handTop` has `height: 272px` fixed. At 1440 the foot is 715px inside a 948px content box, so it will not wrap; verify at 1280 and 1080 that a wrapped second row does not overflow the fixed height, and raise the height once for all cards rather than letting it flex.
2. Assert it. Extend the existing shared-column check at notes-interaction-check.mjs:1013 to run `?state=review` against `.handTop`, and add one assertion that `.handTop`'s left and width are byte-identical across card 1, card 2 after K, and card 1 with the peel open — the horizontal twin of the fixed height the file already argues for in its own comment.

confirmed.element: .idxText[data-clamped]::after, inside the max-width:700px block of master.css — ?state=notebook at 360, 390 and 414
confirmed.problem: On the phone all 14 rows are clamped, and the clamp mark is an absolutely positioned pseudo pinned to right:0 with an 18px-wide white gradient. The gradient is far too short to hide the cut, so the last word renders as a half glyph — "Bring the worke⟨d sliced⟩" — and the ellipsis that belongs to it sits 30 to 160px away in its own column (measured: last line ends at x=205, the ellipsis box starts at x=339, box right edge 365). Fourteen times per screen the densest object in the product shows a chopped letterform and a floating ellipsis that reads as a separate element. This is the standing checklist's mid-word cut, live on the surface the locked architecture says capture happens on, and the desktop word-safe trim never runs here because the mobile path is pure CSS overflow.
confirmed.fix: Delete the ::after and its gradient, and extend the existing JS trim to the two-line mobile box: after paint, while text.scrollHeight > text.clientHeight, pop whole words off the preview span and re-measure, then write the ellipsis as the last inline character of the text itself — text.innerHTML = `${lede} ${words.join(" ")}…` — using the same resize re-run and the same never-below-the-lede floor the desktop trim already has, and leaving data-full untouched so the accessible name keeps the whole sentence. If the pseudo must survive, replace it with mask-image: linear-gradient(90deg, #000 calc(100% - 52px), transparent) on .idxText itself so the fade is continuous across the whole last line, and never a hard edge mid-glyph.
confirmed.verdict: CONFIRMED, with the finding's measurements corrected. Verified live in Playwright at 360, 390 and 414: all 14 index rows carry data-clamped at every phone width. The .idxText[data-clamped]::after is 27px wide (18px padding-left + 8.97px for the ellipsis glyph) and its gradient reaches FULL opacity at 40%, so it paints solid white from boxRight-16.2px to boxRight. Measured distance from the last visible glyph to the box edge at 390: 12.2, 12.2, 4.2, 9.3, 15.3, 5.4, 23.6, 8.9, 18.7, 22.1, 9.1, 24.2, 21.5, 26.5. Seven of fourteen rows have glyphs under the opaque region. Screenshot of row 3 at rest reads "Bring the worke" plus a half-erased d, then a 14px void, then a detached "…". The remaining rows escape the slice but still show the ellipsis as a separate floating cluster 12 to 18px off the end of the sentence, reading as a fourth column rather than punctuation. Decisive: the SAME row on hover, where the existing rule ".idxRow:hover .idxText[data-clamped]::after { background: none }" fires, renders "Bring the worked …" — whole word, ellipsis hard against the text, one continuous line. The artifact already contains the correct rendering; the gradient is the only difference, and the state a person actually looks at is the broken one, thirteen rows out of fourteen. This is the standing checklist's "clamps that cut mid-word", live on the phone, which is the surface the locked architecture says capture happens on. Not covered by the measured baseline: notes-audit checks palette, weights, contrast, hit targets, radii and motion, none of which see a gradient overlay; notes-interaction-check's word-safe-trim assertions exercise the desktop nowrap path in trimRows(), which explicitly `continue`s out on mobile after only setting data-clamped. data-full is untouched, so this is a purely visual defect, not an accessible-name one. The finding's own numbers are wrong and should not be quoted: no row ends at x=205 (the range is 338 to 361), and the separation is 0 to 18px, not 30 to 160. The 339/365 figure for the pseudo box is correct. Its second, fallback fix must be rejected outright — mask-image on .idxText applies to the whole element box, so it would fade the right 52px of line ONE as well, which is complete text with nothing trimmed from it, making a clean line look damaged to hide a damaged one. That half would make the work worse.
confirmed.sharpenedFix: Delete .idxText[data-clamped]::after, its gradient, and the two hover/cursor overrides that exist only to undo it. Extend the existing trimRows() word-safe trim to the mobile two-line box instead of bailing out of it: in the branch where getComputedStyle(text).whiteSpace !== "nowrap", keep setting data-clamped for anything that needs to know, but then run the same loop the desktop path already runs, measuring height instead of width — rebuild the row as `lede rest`, and while text.scrollHeight > text.clientHeight + 1 pop one whole word off the preview span and re-measure, writing the ellipsis as the last inline character of the text itself so it inherits ink-3 and sits hard against the final word. Reuse the floor the desktop trim already enforces: never cut into the lede, never below the first four words. It already re-runs on fonts.ready and on resize, and data-full stays untouched, so the accessible name keeps the whole sentence. The target rendering is not hypothetical — it is exactly what the hover state of these rows renders today ("Bring the worked …"), so the fix is to make the resting state match the state the file already draws correctly. Do NOT take the mask-image alternative: a mask on .idxText fades the right edge of line one too, where nothing has been trimmed.

confirmed.element: .idxText b — ?state=notebook (14 of 14 rows) and ?state=pressure (36 of 36)
confirmed.problem: The 600 lede is meant to be one earned budget, but every note in the corpus clears the 48-character complete-sentence test, so 100 percent of rows open in semibold. Under pressure that is ten bold runs stacked in one viewport and three of them are the same sentence. A weight paid on every row is not emphasis, it is the body weight of the plane — and it is the same 600 the day heading uses, so the index has one weight doing headings, ledes and search hits at once. The rule is true of the code and false of the artifact.
confirmed.fix: Keep the 48-character sentence rule but stop paying it in weight. Set .idxText b to font-weight: 400 with color: var(--ink-1) and leave .idxText span at var(--ink-2) — the density split the palette already owns — so the lede reads as the darker half of one sentence rather than a different typeface. Reserve 600 in the index for exactly two things: the row under the keyboard cursor and a search hit. Then measure it: load ?state=pressure and count semibold runs on screen; more than three means the emphasis is spent again.
confirmed.verdict: CONFIRMED by driving the file. Row counts are exact: notebook 14/14 and pressure 36/36 render a <b>; every one of the 10 rows in the 1440x960 pressure viewport opens semibold, and they are three sentences repeated three times each. 67% of rendered index glyphs are 600, which is the same two-thirds share the source comment at notebook.js:206-221 says the 88-character version was rejected for. Worse than the finding states: the 48-character rule (LEDE_MAX, notebook.js:222) governs only makeNote, i.e. typed capture. The corpus derives its lede at data.js:241 with an uncapped split on terminal punctuation and never sets a `lede` field, so `note.lede === false` is never true at notebook.js:1199 and no rendered row is subject to the rule at all. Consequence: 2 notebook rows and 6 pressure rows are 600 end to end with no 400 half, one of them 105 characters, which is the exact inversion of the stated rule that an unqualified row renders whole at 400. The voice keep-both path (notebook.js:2066) repeats the same uncapped split. Not a restatement of the measured baseline, which gates the weight set {400,600} but not its distribution. Adds no hue and no weight, so it breaks no constraint; moving the preview from ink-3 to ink-2 raises contrast rather than lowering it. Only inaccuracy in the finding is minor: search hits are <mark> with indigo-wash (master.css:588), not 600, so 600 is currently doing group headings and ledes, not hits.
confirmed.sharpenedFix: Fix the derivation before the CSS, or the CSS change hides a second bug. (1) One lede function: delete the ad-hoc `body.split(/(?<=[.?!”])\s/)[0]` at data.js:241 and notebook.js:2066 and route all three call sites through ledeOf, setting `lede` explicitly so an unqualified body takes the `lede === false` path and renders whole. That alone kills the 105-character all-semibold rows and drops the corpus well below 14/14. (2) Then stop paying the earned lede in weight: `.idxText b { font-weight: 400; color: var(--ink-1) }` and `.idxText span { color: var(--ink-2) }`, so the lede is the darker half of one sentence rather than a second typeface. Leave 600 in the index plane to the group heading alone; do not reserve it for the search hit, which already has its own indigo-wash mark and would end up with two treatments. If the keyboard cursor needs more at rest than its ink tint, give it fill, not weight. confirmed.element: ?state=seam receipt line, data.js:343 stayedPut, concatenated with sentReceipt into #say

Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." Two defects in one string. The same fact is stated twice in two grammars in a single announcement. And the claim is false: driven across three notes on the desk, .readBody carries zero textareas and zero contenteditable nodes, the More control beside the primary is inert, and no surface anywhere in the master lets a kept note be changed. Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." Source: notebook.js:680 `say(`${N.copy.sentReceipt} ${N.copy.stayedPut}`)`, concatenating data.js:344 ("Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here.") with data.js:343. "Your note stayed here" and "Your note is still here" are the same proposition in two grammars, spoken back-to-back in a single live-region utterance, at the one moment in the product where trust in the one-way edge is either won or lost. That is precisely the standing-checklist defect ("facts stated in two grammars"), and it is not covered by the measured baseline: notes-interaction-check.mjs:461 counts privacy promises only in `.top` and only BEFORE the send; line 704 merely asserts the announcement *includes* "Your note stayed here", which is what lets the duplicate through. Cutting it, as proposed, removes the only sentence that says the send did not take ownership. The proposed replacement announcement ("and only those words crossed") also re-states the boundary a third time, which is the same disease the finding is diagnosing.

Say the fact once: replace notebook.js:680 with `say(`${N.copy.confirmed}. ${N.copy.stayedPut}`)` so the spoken line reads "Tasks has it. Your note is still here, still private, still yours to edit." — the headline the receipt already draws, then the three clauses, no proposition twice. `sentReceipt` stays as-is for the hand at line 671, where it is followed by a count rather than by `stayedPut` and reads correctly. Update notes-interaction-check.mjs:704 to assert the announcement carries the promise exactly once (match `/still here|stayed here/g` on `#say` and require length 1) rather than asserting it contains "Your note stayed here", so the gate defends the fix instead of the defect. Nothing in notes-interaction-check.mjs's pressure blocks (354, 538, 869, 1007, 1095, 1192, 1551) asserts anything about body length, so the 333-assertion gate does not cover this. Not a restatement of the measured baseline, not taste, breaks no constraint.

The finding's own fix is wrong twice and must not be applied as written. `n.words > 150` still misses (LONG_BODY is ~148 words), and no threshold can work because `long` is not in the pressure list at all.

But in ?state=nothing there is no .topFoot and no .topMeta (both measured null): the empty state is a headline at 285–1237, a body at 285–812 and two left-aligned first-move buttons ending at 848. The master.css quotation is misapplied. The comment condemns "a 1262px card holding a 527px column" — a card 2.4x its only content. Judging that as dead white proves too much: it condemns the resting capture surface of Bear, iA Writer, Things and Linear's create sheet equally. The capture frame confirms it optically — placeholder or two lines of ink top-left, verb cluster bottom-left, counter and primary bottom-right, balanced.

The fix would also make the work worse on the direction's own terms. The margin's stated rule in master.css is "everything that is true ABOUT the writing goes in a margin beside it"; before anything is written nothing is true about it, so a resting margin is a category error, and Dictate / Read a photo are capture entrances, not facts, which would give one region two grammars. refuted.why:
REFUTED. The measurement is right and everything built on it is wrong.

Measured (Playwright, ?v=locked, .top padding-left 24px): 1440 → .top 261, .topField 285, .readBody 285, .idxText 294. Same 9px at 1280 (181/205/214) and 1920 (501/525/534) and at 768 (110/134/143). So the 9px exists.

1. The behavioural argument is false. notebook.js flyWords() is handed `to = rowEl.querySelector(".idxText").getBoundingClientRect()` and animates `translate(dx…)` where `dx = to.left - from.left`. The words land ON the row's own text axis, exactly, because the destination is read live from that element. The 9px is not a snap at the end of the flight, it IS part of the flight — 9px of lateral travel inside a 520ms cubic-bezier over a ~300px vertical drop, invisible as a discrete event. The row is even held at opacity 0 until 470ms so the handoff is single-printed. The one real discontinuity is 2px, not 9: the ghost is placed at the field's box left (285) while the textarea's UA 2px padding put the glyphs at 287 — and the field is emptied in the same frame, so there is nothing left on screen to compare it against.

2. The second half is fiction. "Lifting a note back onto the desk snaps it 9px the other way" — openNote() sets openId and calls paint(). There is no shared-element travel on the lift at all, no ghost, no transform. Nothing moves laterally, so nothing can snap. A claim about a motion that does not exist.

3. The fix breaks two of the four finished rooms. .idxRow's column-gap is 13px in locked and studio but 11px in quiet and press, so the index's text axis is 294 in two rooms and 292 in the other two. A literal 33px paper padding aligns in locked/studio and misaligns by 2px in quiet/press — it trades one consistent, explicable 9px offset for a room-dependent 0/2px wobble, and hard-couples the paper's margin to the row's mark geometry so any future change to the mark silently de-aligns the desk. The proposed assertion is also wrong on its own terms: it tests computed left of .topField, which carries the textarea's 2px UA padding, so it would go green with the field's actual glyphs sitting 2px off .readBody and .idxText — false precision in exactly the state the finding calls the signature moment.

4. What is left is taste with no argument. Both planes already share --stack, and the paper's edge sits on the mark column (261 = 261). The desk's text is inset because paper has a margin; the row's text is inset because the row has a mark. Those are different reasons to inset, not a broken law, and the build has already chosen the stronger of the two available alignments. "Small enough to read as sloppiness" is an assertion, not evidence.

If a later round still wants the two text axes to coincide, it cannot be 33px: it would have to be derived (calc of the mark width plus the row's gap token) so it holds in all four rooms, and it would have to be asserted on glyph position, not on .topField's box.

refuted.problem: The group heading is separated from the sentences under it by two pixels and nothing else: same weight, same ink, same case, same family. On the phone even that goes — .idxDay steps to --t-15 while .idxText b is already 15/600, so "Mara & Finn" the heading and "…Mara & Finn." the lede 40px below it are typographically identical, and the same words appear three times in the top 330px in three roles at nearly one setting. Bear and Things both separate a list heading from a list item by category, never by a size step. The phone step-down also changes size without stepping tracking, so .idxDay carries --tr-18 (-0.021em) at 15px, off its own curve.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the measured file, on three counts.

1) The central premise is factually false. "Separated by two pixels and nothing else: same weight, same ink, same case, same family" ignores everything the heading actually carries. Measured live at 1440 and at 390, .idxDay and only .idxDay carries: a sticky white band (position: sticky, top 0, z-index 2, background var(--white)); a 1px hairline rule at its foot (::after, rgba(17,17,17,0.055)); a 15px lead-out gradient below that rule (::before, white to transparent) so a row dissolves into it rather than being sliced; 20px of lead-in (16px on phone); an inline companion at 13px/ink-3 sentence case (.idxDayNote, measured 13px 600 rgba(.72) desktop, 12px phone); and a right-aligned 12px/400/ink-3 tail count. And the rows it heads are indented from it: heading left 261 vs lede left 294 desktop (33px), 25 vs 57 on the phone (32px). That is separation by category — band, rule, indent, companion metadata — which is precisely the Bear/Things pattern the finding cites as the standard being missed. It is already the standard being met.

2) The proposed fix reverts a fix a previous round already paid for, and lands worse than the pre-fix state. master.css carries the note in the file: "The subject rule … was set thirteen percent SMALLER than the rows beneath it, in the same weight and the same ink. It leads now." Setting .idxDay to --t-13/ink-3 puts the group heading two steps SMALLER and one ink level LIGHTER than the 15/600/ink-1 lede it heads — a stronger version of exactly the defect that was corrected. It also collides with .indexHead directly above it, which is already 11/600/--tr-cap/uppercase/ink-3: two uppercase micro-labels 30px apart differing by 2px is a worse register collision than the one alleged. And it uppercases user content — the group heading in the default "What it is about" mode is a couple's name, so the fix renders MARA & FINN on a wedding product whose copy rule is sentence case. It further breaks the heading's ink-density state model (.idxDay[data-soon] ink-1 / [data-undated] ink-2, measured rgb(17,17,17) vs rgba(.72)), which is how this surface says which date the house is facing without a second hue.

3) The supporting claims are overstated. Desktop: the three "Mara & Finn" occurrences in the top 330px measure at 15/600/ink-1 (head), 13/400/ink-2 (desk source line) and 17/600/ink-1 (heading) — three distinct settings, not "nearly one". The heading-to-lede gap is 62px, not 40. The tracking sub-claim is real but trivial and off no enforced curve: master.css already sets 15px at --tr-16 (.headNext b, .topField) and at --tr-14 (.idxText), so there is no 1:1 size-to-tracking mapping in the file, the measured gate accepts any declared step, and the delta at 15px is 0.135px per character.

Underneath it, the request that "600/ink-1 mean one thing in the plane" cannot be met under the locked constraint of two weights only: with 400 and 600 the only registers available, 600 must serve both the earned lede and the group heading, and the file separates them by size, band, rule, indent and companion instead. The one grain worth naming — on the phone the head's "Mara & Finn" (.headNext b, 15/600/ink-1) and the group heading are identical type 70px apart — is a different element the proposed fix does not touch, and they sit in different planes across an uppercase "YOUR NOTES" head and the group control.

refuted.problem: "Yours until you send something on" is printed while the sheet is empty and removed the moment there is something private on it. In its place appears "16 / 4000" — a limit stated from the sixteenth character, machine-facing, of no use to a person writing a thought. On the phone it degrades to a bare "40" floating in the dock with no unit and no context. The product's second promise is shown only when it has nothing to promise about, and the pixel it is traded for is engineering furniture.
refuted.why: The central claim is factually wrong. The privacy promise is not evicted: notebook.js:898 renders a permanent head control in every state and at every width, visible text "Private to you" with accessible name "Private to you. Yours until you send something on." I confirmed it live at 1440 in idle, in the live/count state, and past 4000 characters, and at 390 on the phone (visible at 202,18); both the locked-notebook and locked-capture frames show it top-right, ~25px above the foot slot in dispute. What the count replaces is a second, longer printing of a promise that never leaves the sheet, shown at idle where it does first-contact reassurance before the first word and retired once the row is needed for the act. The proposed fix is also worse on two counts: (1) it makes the doubling permanent, stating one fact in two grammars in the same right-hand column 25px apart, which is a named item on the standing checklist; (2) it does not fit. Measured .topFoot in the live state, the spacer slack is 175px at 1440 and 1180 but 77px at 1080, while a nowrap .topMeta carrying "Yours until you send something on" measures 185px, so a permanent fixed right-hand slot alongside the count and "Save it Ctrl+Enter" overflows the foot at the gated 1080 fold width. On the phone, .dockCount is aria-hidden="true", so "no unit and no context" never reaches assistive tech; it is a decorative 11px tint beside the field being typed into.

refuted.problem: The same string is printed twice inside one viewport, 380 pixels apart, in the same words and the same order, and both are inert text. Nothing tells a stranger that one is what the house is facing and the other is a pile of notes; nothing connects them. Two days before the wedding the notebook states the wedding in its largest type and offers no way to act on it — the venue owner cannot ask the product the only question she has, which is "show me Saturday".
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440 (?state=notebook&v=locked) and at ?state=pressure, plus master.css and notebook.js read. The only true part is the bare duplication; every claim the finding builds on it is wrong, and the fix would break a gated assertion and delete the better of the two instances.

1. The hierarchy claim is inverted. Measured: `.headNext b` = 15px/600, `.headNext span` = 13px/400 at y=38. `.idxDay` = 17px/600 at y=305 (gap is 267 CSS px, not 380). The notebook's largest type is 17px — the wordmark and the INDEX group rule. So "the notebook states the wedding in its largest type and offers no way to act on it" is describing the index heading, which is the thing the finding proposes to DELETE, while the instance it proposes to convert into a filter is the smaller, quieter one. The finding wants to keep the 15px echo in the chrome band and drop the 17px rule that also carries the group's own pending count ("1 still to decide", "3" under pressure). That is keeping the weaker copy.

2. "Nothing tells a stranger that one is what the house is facing and the other is a pile of notes; nothing connects them" is false against the rendered DOM. The index instance sits directly under a labelled band — `.indexHead` prints "Your notes · 14 notes" followed by the lit `groupBtn` "What it is about" (aria-pressed=true) beside "When". That band states, in the product's own words, that the rules below are subject groups of the pile. The head instance sits in the chrome row with the wordmark, the workspace name "The Orchard, events", the chip and "Private to you". Two visibly different registers, each framed.

3. "The venue owner cannot ask the product 'show me Saturday'" is false in effect. The default grouping is `group = "about"`, and `groupsOf()` sorts by stake then days, so the couple's notes are already gathered, first in the pile, under one rule carrying their own count. That is the answer to "show me Saturday", delivered with no mode to enter and no mode to leave, and it is why the rules exist (data.js:56-75). Toggling "When" removes the duplicate entirely (verified: index heads become Today/Yesterday/Monday/Sunday/Saturday) — so the "collision" is a consequence of a first-class visible control the product ships, not an unanswered question. The proposed filter adds a third scope mechanism alongside grouping and search.

4. The fix breaks the gate and gets its own number wrong. "Scopes the chip to '3 still to decide about Mara & Finn'": in ?state=notebook the couple-scoped pending count is 1, not 3 (3 is the pressure fixture). More seriously, notes-interaction-check.mjs round 6 asserts "the head does not print the chip's phrase beside the chip" (`!lede.includes("still to decide")`) and "the chip names its own scope … across the whole notebook". Re-scoping the chip to the couple reinstates the exact two-counts-in-one-line stutter round 6 paid to remove, and fails a standing assertion.

5. Residue, for the record, narrower than the finding: "Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" does render verbatim twice at rest, and by construction always will while grouping is "about" (N.next is hardcoded to the one stake-1 subject, which always sorts first). If a seat wants to act on it, the edit is on the head — drop or shorten the head's date clause when the first group rule is already printing it — not a new filter mode, and never on the index rule that carries the count. As stated, the finding is a misread of the hierarchy attached to a fix that is a net loss.

refuted.problem: The standing privacy line in the head reads "Private to you". That string does not exist in notes-copy.ts. The product's own word is privacyAssurance: "Private until you send it on" — conditional, because the product is a one-way edge into Tasks and the promise is only true until you use it. The lab replaced the conditional with an absolute and then printed the honest version thirteen hundred pixels away on the desk foot ("Yours until you send something on"), so the same screen carries the promise in two grammars, and the louder, lock-badged one is the one that overclaims. data.js's own header says these strings are "Verbatim from notes-copy.ts… No direction may rewrite them"; four have in fact been rewritten (privacyAssurance, wordingLabel → "What the task will say", destinationLabel → "To", voice.stop → "Stop and read it back"). Three of those four are improvements. This one is a regression on the single sentence the venue offer legally rests on.
refuted.why: REFUTED on the source, on measurement, and as a restatement. 1. "Private to you" is not a lab invention. It is the SHIPPED header string, verbatim: src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:909 renders `Private to you` in the same header slot, with the same lock glyph and the same sibling "Notes options" button as the lab's `.headAct[data-act="privacy"]`. The lab mirrors the product's own header 1:1. It is absent from notes-copy.ts because notes-copy.ts governs the capture and hand-off flow, not the header badge — grep confirms `capture.privacyAssurance` and `capture.headerAssurance` have zero call sites in NotesWorkspace.tsx. The proposed fix would make the lab DIVERGE from the shipped product on the one string the finding says the offer legally rests on. 2. The conditional promise is ALREADY in the accessible name the finding asks for it to be added to. Driven live at 1440x960 in Playwright across ?state=notebook, seam and voice, the chip's aria-label reads, in all three: "Private to you. Yours until you send something on." The finding proposes an aria-label carrying the conditional clause. It is already there, word for word, in the second half. 3. The "thirteen hundred pixels away" measurement is false by an order of magnitude. Measured getBoundingClientRect().top: head chip 32, `.topMeta` "Yours until you send something on" 199. That is 167px, same fold, badge directly above its own expansion — a title and its subclause, not two grammars at opposite ends of a screen. And that foot line IS the product's own conditional, rendered verbatim (notes-copy.ts:172 headerAssurance), so the honest sentence is on screen, adjacent, not exiled. 4. The proposed swap puts a string in the wrong slot. notes-copy.ts documents `capture.privacyAssurance` ("Private until you send it on") as the standing line next to the CAPTURE label, and `capture.headerAssurance` as the header string. The fix asks for the capture string in the header slot while the header string is already rendered in the capture foot — i.e. it would swap two correctly-placed strings into each other's wrong slots. 5. Three of the four "rewritten" keys are factually wrong about data.js, which the finding names as the culprit. data.js:327/335/336 read `voiceStop: "Stop listening"`, `destinationLabel: "Which project"`, `wordingLabel: "The task wording"` — all three verbatim from the generic register. Those were fixed in an earlier round. (The seam does render "What the task will say" and "To", and voice renders "Stop and read it back", from notebook.js at render time — but "What the task will say" is itself verbatim from notes-copy.ts's WEDDING register at :272, and the fixture's own comment permits a direction to decide where a string lives. The finding's account of the mechanism and of the file is wrong regardless.) 6. It is a restatement three times over. log.html:670, :1332 and :1997 each refuse this exact premise against the same NotesWorkspace header citation, and :1332 already refuted a near-identical "every rendered string must equal a copy-module value" gate on the ground that data.js is a shared fixture read by render-a/b/c and notebook.js, so such a gate would force strings into slots whose fact they do not state. The brief's own settled list also carries "No privacy claim stronger than the product's own conditional promise, anywhere" — this finding restates it. The fix would make the work worse: it deletes a string the shipped product uses, moves two correctly-slotted strings into each other's slots, and adds a gate three of whose four premises are false.

refuted.problem: The strongest mark the three-colour lock permits is solid ink at full density, and it is spent on a chore counter. "8 still to decide" is a black pill and it is the loudest object on a white sheet whose entire promise is the three seconds between a thought and safety. It outranks the venue's name, the wedding two days out, and the words the person is actually writing, and it stays lit through the dictation return and through the middle of the seam, where the person is deciding what crosses. The product's own reassurance in the hand — "Nothing is decided until you say so" — is set in ink-3 at 13px; the nag is set in white on full ink. The ink is being obeyed, not spent.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440x960 across all ten states, plus master.css:265-275 and notebook.js:886-900.

1. The finding's central proof is a juxtaposition that never renders. It contrasts "the nag set in white on full ink" against "the product's own reassurance in the hand — 'Nothing is decided until you say so' — set in ink-3 at 13px." That sentence is `.deckNote`, and it exists ONLY in the review room. notebook.js:888 reads `state === "review" ? "" : ...` — the chip is already suppressed in exactly the room where the hand and that sentence live. Measured: `?state=review` returns chip `null`. The two objects the finding puts side by side are never on screen together.

2. "It stays lit through the dictation return" is wrong at the takeover. In `?state=voice` the head is covered by `.darkBody` (elementFromPoint at the chip's centre returns `darkBody/DIV`) and `.sheet` carries `inert`. The chip is neither lit nor reachable while she is dictating. It is present in readback, but readback is the sheet, not the takeover — she is back in the notebook.

3. Half the proposed fix is already the build. "Reserve full-ink fill for the one control that commits the person's words" is precisely what `.act[data-ink]` already is, and the only thing it is: Save it, Keep both, Write the first one, Open that one, Delete (inverted to white-on-ink in the destroy room, master.css:964). Every ink fill in the product other than the chip is a commit primary. The finding proposes as a correction the rule the file already obeys.

4. "The loudest object on a white sheet" does not survive measurement at the moment that matters. Mid-thought (`?state=capture`) the Save it primary is 5961px² at 13px against the chip's 2842px² at 12px — more than twice the area, on the paper, at the eye's centre, while the chip is a 26px pill at the top edge of a 62px head. In readback the ink primary is 4123px² against the same 2842px². In the resting notebook the chip is the only fill, but it is 2842px² of a 1440x960 composition whose index carries sixteen rows of bold 15px ink-1 — it is the smallest text in the head, last in its reading order, not first.

5. "It outranks the venue's name and the wedding two days out" misreads a deliberate two-channel head. The head is ordered by importance left to right: wordmark, house (`The Orchard, events`, ink-2/400 by design — it is the label, not the news), then the wedding as the lead fact at 15px/600 ink-1 with its date, then the count. The chip emphasises by fill; the wedding emphasises by size, weight and position. Reading order gives the wedding the lead, and the chip is the last thing before the chrome.

6. The demotion would make the work worse. `chip[data-off]` already exists as exactly the register the finding asks for — no fill, ink-2, hairline inset, weight 400. Moving the live count into it collapses the one route into the decision queue to the same register as the `.headAct` chrome (Private to you, options) and the same drawn treatment as the sixteen "To decide" row markers below it. The only object in the notebook that says something is outstanding would become indistinguishable from a settings button. That is a legible hierarchy traded for an even one.

What is left is a taste position — that fill should mean act, not count — argued with a composite screenshot nobody sees, against a rule already implemented, with a fix that flattens the head. Not a defect at the 9.5 bar.

refuted.problem: The one gesture that makes this Notes and not Bear — a second, smaller piece of paper peeling off the note — is explicitly deleted on the primary surface. In the review hand the peel is real: it has its own edge, its own shadow, and a notch pointing back at the card it came from, and it is the best moment in the build. On the desk, where almost everyone will meet the seam, the same component is stripped of shadow, notch and padding and becomes a flat right-hand column separated by a hairline. It reads as a share sidebar, not as paper. The comment in the stylesheet states the reason outright: "so the sheet's lower third is not left empty." The product traded its signature idea for a layout convenience. The whole file also carries only two @keyframes — `arrive` and `recPulse` — so nothing about paper lifting, peeling or crossing is ever played anywhere; the metaphor is asserted in copy and drawn only once, in the room fewest people open.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Three of the finding's load-bearing claims are false against the source, and the proposed fix visibly degrades the surface when applied.

1. "Drawn only once, in the room fewest people open" is wrong. master.css:664 is `.phoneSheetBody .peel { width:100%; margin:12px 0 0 }` and :665 kills only the notch — it does NOT reset box-shadow or padding. On the phone, where the couples in this product's audience meet the seam, the peel keeps `border-radius: var(--r-paper)`, `box-shadow: var(--ring), var(--paper)` and `padding: 15px 17px 16px` from :880-883. So the signature gesture is drawn as real paper in the hand AND on the phone; the two-column desk is the only place it folds into the margin.

2. "Only two @keyframes, so nothing about paper lifting, peeling or crossing is ever played anywhere" mistakes an implementation technique for an absence. Paper motion in this build runs on transitions, not keyframes: :378 `.top { transition: box-shadow/transform/opacity var(--dur-settle) }` with :379 `.top[data-settling] { transform: translateY(14px) scale(0.972); opacity: 0 }` — the sheet physically leaves for the pile; :763 `.handTop[data-settling] { transform: translateY(-14px) scale(0.985); opacity: 0 }` — the card lifts off the hand; :750-752 the `.handCard[data-n]` stack transforms. Counting `@keyframes` blocks is not counting motion.

3. The stylesheet comment is quoted selectively. :885-886 reads "Inside the desk's own margin, so the note and the task it is becoming are side by side AND the sheet's lower third is not left empty." The first clause is the architectural reason and it matches :309-312 ("everything that is true ABOUT the writing goes in a margin beside it, which is also where the peel opens"). The finding drops that clause and presents the second as "the reason ... stated outright", then calls a considered composition a "layout convenience".

The measured geometry also contradicts "flat right-hand column" as a size complaint: at 1440 ?state=seam the desk peel is 392px wide against a 496px writing column — already the smaller of the two, inside the note's own paper, and never covering it.

Most decisively, I applied the proposed fix live at 1440 (width: calc(100% - 10px); margin: 0 0 0 10px; ring + paper shadow; r-paper; notch at left:-7px top:34px) and screenshotted before/after. It is worse: (a) the peel becomes a floating white card nested inside the desk's white card, growing 259px to 290px tall and running to within ~10px of the sheet's right and bottom edges, so the sheet's own margin is broken and the panel reads as a popover, not as paper peeled off; (b) `.deskAside` still carries `box-shadow: inset 1px 0 0 var(--line-soft)` (:329), which the fix does not remove, so the column rule is left orphaned 30px to the left of the new card — a doubled frame; (c) the notch, whose shadow is `-1px -1px 0 var(--line)` (lit on top and left, drawn for a downward-pointing tab), at left:-7px lights the wrong two edges and points into an empty 34px gutter rather than at the picked sentence, which sits on line two at the far left of the note.

The added `peel` keyframe is also a hazard, not a gain: startPeel sets `refocus = { kind: "field", sel: ".peelField" }` (notebook.js), so the panel takes the caret on open. Translating a container 10px on the X axis while a textarea inside it receives focus is a scroll-anchor and caret-placement risk on the one surface whose whole job is to let a person check the exact words before they cross.

What is left after the false claims are removed is a bare taste preference — "the widest desk should render the peel as a detached sheet" — with no argument that survives the pixels, against an architecture line the current build already honours ("the note is never covered") and a two-column desk composition the file argues for explicitly.

refuted.problem: At 36 notes the index is a uniform wall. Every row is the same height, the same weight structure and the same tint; a group can hold nine rows spanning 23 minutes to 12 hours with no rule, no thinning, no fold, nothing to navigate by but scrolling. A working venue owner will pass 36 notes in a fortnight and 300 in a season, and this plane has exactly one answer for that: search. That is the point at which the product stops being a notebook that knows its owner and becomes a list. It is also the state where the whole architecture of desk-and-index has to pay off, and it does not — the index below 36 rows feels no different from the index below 5.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the source, and the fix is inert at the state it targets. (1) All 36 pressure notes have n.day === "Today" — verified by driving ?state=pressure&group=day, which yields ONE group headed "Today". The proposed "hairline day rule whenever n.day changes between consecutive rows" would draw zero rules at pressure. (2) The day axis is not missing: groupControl() (notebook.js:1267) paints a segmented "What it is about" / "When" toggle in the index head, visible in locked-pressure--1440x960.png, announced live, and scroll-preserving (scrollTop 600 held across the repaint). (3) "No rule" is false: master.css:554 .idxRow + .idxRow::before draws a 1px var(--line-soft) hairline between every consecutive pair, and each group head is a sticky var(--t-17)/600 rule a full step above the 15px rows with its own ::after hairline and a 15px lead-out gradient. (4) "Drop the rest text to var(--ink-3)" is already shipped: .idxText span { color: var(--ink-3) } (master.css:582), measured rgba(17,17,17,0.62) on every row. (5) "Same weight structure" is false: 6 of 13 rows in "The studio" are lede-less, one weight end to end; heads vary by data-soon (--ink-1, 600 note) vs data-undated (--ink-2) and carry the facing date plus an "N still to decide" tail; rows carry source glyph, pending dot, tag and time columns. (6) The fold would make it worse: only one group exceeds 12 rows (13), so it hides exactly one row and prints "1 older" — a second count in a plane whose count discipline is gated (head/index agreement, one object owns each count), and it contradicts the locked architecture's "everything older, one line each", which every 40px row already satisfies. What remains is the unargued taste claim that the register does not change between 14 and 36 rows, contradicted by the file's two grouping axes, stake ordering, per-group facing dates and decide-counts, tags, search and the arrow walk.

refuted.problem: The product has two orderings of one pile and the deciding surface uses the weaker one. The index knows the house's clock — it sorts Mara & Finn to the top because stake is 1 and the date is two days out — and the head prints "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days". The hand, which is where the decisions actually get made, deals oldest-first with no reference to stake or days: card 1 is the Saturday ballroom question, card 2 is a no-date idea for the studio newsletter, and the two remaining Saturday decisions sit behind it. So the one fact that makes this Notes-for-a-venue rather than Notes is displayed everywhere and operative nowhere in the room built to act on it. This is precisely the "well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words" reading, and it is one comparator wide.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the fixture on two counts, and its central charge is disproved by the artifact. (1) The hand does not deal "oldest-first" — it deals NEWEST-first: driven at ?state=review, cards 1-5 read 3 hours ago, 5 hours ago, 6 hours ago, 9 hours ago, Yesterday. Direction reversed. (2) "the two remaining Saturday decisions sit behind it" is false: n01 and n02 are `sent: true` (already in Tasks, not pending, not in queue()). Exactly ONE Mara & Finn note is pending, and it is card 1 — "Ask the venue whether the ballroom can be accessed from 8am on the Saturday" (about: mara-finn, stake 1, days 2). So the deciding surface already opens on the highest-stake, nearest-dated note; the claim that the venue's clock is "operative nowhere in the room built to act on it" is contradicted by the first card the room deals. Applying the proposed comparator to the shipped fixture moves exactly one card — n06 (the course, stake 2, days 0) from position 4 to position 2 — and leaves card 1 identical. The fix would also make it worse where it bites: stake outranks days in groupsOf, so as a deal order it hands the person a Mara & Finn item two days out ahead of a course deadline due TODAY; that comparator was written to order groups ("the house's business first"), not to rank individual cards against each other. refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's load-bearing evidence was measured on the wrong entry path, two of its three fixes are already shipped or actively harmful, and one of them would break a gated assertion a previous round deliberately established.

1) "document.activeElement is BODY on entry" — measured on the lab deep-link `?state=voice`, not the product path. Driven live: entering via the verb (`.verb[data-act="voice"]`) puts `activeElement` on `BUTTON|voice-stop|darkAct`. notebook.js:2041 already does exactly what the fix proposes: `refocus = { kind: "act", sel: '[data-act="voice-stop"]' }`. Worse, the proposed selector is `'[data-act="stop"]'`, which matches nothing in the file — applying the fix as written would delete the working focus placement and produce the very BODY-focus bug it claims to fix.

2) "the way out is an untargeted Tab away and the microphone is live with the keyboard nowhere" — false. notebook.js:2245 collects the takeover's stops and notes-interaction-check.mjs:740-762 already gates a full round-trip trap: focus lands on voice-stop, six Tabs never leave `.dark`, Shift+Tab stays inside, Escape exits with "Nothing was kept." Restating that is restating the measured baseline.

3) "tells a non-looking user none of it" — false on three counts. `say("Listening. Speak whenever you are ready. Stop when you are done.")` fires into the polite `sr` region on entry (verified live: sr text present via click, gated at check line 304). The sheet and rail get `inert` (notebook.js:1804), which removes the background from the accessibility tree outright — a stronger guarantee than `aria-modal`, which is advisory only. And the container is `<section aria-label="Dictating">`, which maps to a named region, not the "plain div"/"generic" the finding describes.

4) The `.darkSaid` change is the part that would make the work worse. `role="status"` is `aria-live="polite"` — polite regions queue and wait for a pause; they cannot "interrupt the speaker continuously". Turning it to `aria-live="off"` is the single change that would actually create the checklist defect the finding invokes: a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking, because the words the engine heard would no longer be read back. It also directly violates the gated assertion "the words arrive as a live region, not as decoration" (notes-interaction-check.mjs:311-314), a decision an earlier round paid for.

What survives is thin: the disclosure is not folded into the entry announcement, and `.dark` lacks the `role="dialog" aria-modal="true"` that the sibling `.phoneSheet` (notebook.js:1320) carries. That is a semantic tidy-up, not "a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking" — and it is not worth a finding at a 9.5 bar when the surrounding claim is wrong about the entry path, wrong about the tab trap, wrong about the announcement, proposes a selector that does not exist, and would regress the transcript live region.
